title: Fire Chief
statement:
Here's what I can say on the record, Chief Hollowell, and here's what I can't yet.

**What the sheet shows, plain:**

Twelve engine events across Cycles 100–116. Only four were real fires — Grand Lake (104), BIZ-00055 (107), Laurel (111), Brooklyn (111) were minors, and two contained major blazes: Adams Point (109) and KONO (116). That's six false alarms out of twelve — **50%**. That's the number I'd want to stand behind an engine for, and right now it doesn't.

**The two I'm going to be asked about first:**

- **Cycle 106, BIZ-00059, false alarm — $21.55 of annual revenue.** That's Foothill Builders out of Fruitvale, a 110-employee construction outfit. A truck rolled on nothing. Small dollar figure in the ledger, but it's a real employer in a neighborhood that's already under inflow pressure. That's the kind of call that gets remembered.
- **Cycle 107, BIZ-00055, minor fire — Estuary Architects, Lake Merritt, 45 employees.** Note the revenue field is blank on that business record. Before I talk about dollar impact there, somebody needs to tell me whether that's a data gap or a real zero. I'm not going to cite a loss number I can't see.

**Pattern I care about beyond the false alarms:**

The false alarms cluster where the fog and overcast sit. Cycle 108 had *two* in one cycle — Dimond and Uptown, both under fog. Cycle 110, Chinatown, fog. Cycle 102, Piedmont Ave, cold/overcast. Cycle 100, KONO, mild. And the two major blazes — Adams Point at Cycle 109 and KONO at 116 — both landed on overcast-to-fog stretches too. That's a correlation I want the data shop to run down before I decide whether this is sensor/verification trouble or just coincidence.

**The thing that's actually on my mind:**

**KONO got hit twice** — a false alarm at Cycle 100 and a contained major blaze at 116. Adams Point took a contained major at 109. Chinatown — my own neighborhood — took a false alarm at 110. Sentiment is bleeding a few hundredths off every one of these, and the neighborhoods catching the false alarms are the same ones catching the real ones. People stop trusting the siren when it cries wolf half the time.

**My decision, stated plainly:**

I'm not putting anything further on the record as a finding until the verification/dispatch question is answered. What I will say now is that a 50% false-alarm rate is not a rate I'll defend as normal operations — it's a problem I'm going to own.

**What I need from the data shop before my next statement:**
1. The BIZ-00055 revenue blank — data gap or actual zero.
2. Whether false alarms are coming from *verified* call sources (alarms, automated detection) or third-party reports, broken out by neighborhood.
3. The fog/overcast correlation run properly, not eyeballed like I just did.

I've got nothing on the record yet, and I'd like to keep it that way until those three come back — because the first thing I say about this becomes the story, and I want the story to be right. My family's in Chinatown; I'm not going to stand up and shrug about a siren that's wrong half the time on my own street.
